  <content># AGENTS.md

This file provides guidance to agents when working with code in this repository.

## What this project is
Standup Sync reads a single git repository's commit history over a date range and produces a human-readable summary of what was accomplished — suitable for posting to Slack, sending as an email digest, or reading out in a standup.

The core value-add over existing "changelog bot" tools: instead of just listing commit *messages* (often vague — "fix bug", "wip"), this tool reads the actual *diffs* and infers what changed and why, then groups related commits and flags likely blockers (repeated fixes to the same file, reverts, etc).

## Problem it solves
Developers often work across many small commits with unhelpful messages. Writing a standup update, a Slack progress post, or a status email means manually reconstructing "what did I actually get done" from a messy git log. This tool automates that reconstruction using an LLM that reads real diffs.

## Hackathon context
- Built for the IBM Bob 2.0 Hackathon (lablab.ai), Sept 25–27, 2026.
- IBM Bob must be used meaningfully during development. Take screenshots of Bob's task session summaries as you go, and note below (or in commit messages) which parts Bob generated or substantially assisted with.
- Scope is intentionally single-repo. Multi-repo aggregation is explicitly out of scope for this build — do not add it.
- Deadline is tight (well under 48 hours as of this writing). Bias every decision toward "smallest thing that demos cleanly" over "more complete."

## Core pipeline (in order)
1. **Git extraction** — run `git log -p` over a given date range (default: last 24h) for the target repo, on the local filesystem (clone if given a URL, otherwise use a local path).
2. **Noise filtering** — drop merge commits, formatting-only diffs, and changes to generated/lock files (`package-lock.json`, `*.min.js`, etc.) before anything is sent to the model.
3. **Diff analysis** — send filtered commits/diffs to the LLM in batches; ask it to describe *what changed and why* in plain English, not just restate the commit message.
4. **Grouping** — cluster the per-commit summaries by theme (shared directories/files touched) and by author. Pure logic, no LLM call.
5. **Blocker detection** — flag patterns suggesting a struggle: the same file touched 3+ times in the window, revert commits, or a commit message containing "revert" / "undo" / "wip" / "fix fix". Deterministic pattern-matching only — keep it cheap, fast, and unit-testable.
6. **Summary generation** — produce one structured intermediate summary object (see `architecture.md`) that every output format renders from.
7. **Format rendering** — turn the structured summary into one of:
   - Slack (short, casual, bullet-heavy, light emoji)
   - Email (slightly more formal, grouped by workstream)
   - Standup notes (per-person "what I did / possible blockers")

## Non-goals for this build
- No multi-repo support.
- No scheduled/automated runs (cron, GitHub Action) — manual trigger only.
- No auth, no user accounts, no persistence beyond the current session.
- No Bob-inferred ("smart") semantic classification — grouping uses simple heuristics (shared file paths / directories), not model calls.
- No polished design system — functional UI is enough.

## Conventions for whoever (or whatever agent) builds this
- Keep the noise filter and blocker detector as pure functions with no LLM calls — they must be unit-testable without hitting an API.
- Keep the three output formats as templates over one shared summary object, not three separate pipelines. Adding or tweaking a format should never require touching extraction or analysis code.
- Prefer clarity and a working demo over extensibility. This is a rush build; don't add config systems, plugin architectures, or abstractions that aren't needed for the single-repo case.
- Every LLM prompt used (for diff analysis and summary generation) should live in one clearly named location (e.g. `prompts/`) so it's easy to show judges exactly what was asked of Bob during development and what the running app itself asks the model at runtime — these are two different things and both matter for the submission.
- Fail loudly and simply. If the repo path is invalid or there are no commits in range, show a clear message — don't silently return an empty summary.

## What "done" looks like for the hackathon demo
- Paste a repo path/URL + pick a date range in a simple web UI.
- Click generate, see a before/after view: raw git log vs. the generated summary.
- Toggle between Slack / Email / Standup views of the same underlying data.
- At least one visible example of blocker detection catching something a flat commit list would miss.

## Submission reminders (do not leave until the end)
- Screenshot Bob's task session summaries continuously while building, not retroactively.
- Keep a running one-line log per session of what Bob was asked to do and what it produced (see `tasks.md` for where this fits in the timeline).
- Budget real time (3–4 hours) at the end for: demo video, slides, cover image, deployment, and the actual lablab.ai submission form.

## Rules
- When planning for the project, put any documents and artifacts in the `./plan/` folder.
- Put all deliverables of this project in `./deliverables/`. Deliverables are content, assets, or artifacts to be submitted to the hackathon.
- This project should create/update a `README.md` file that details the following:
  - What this project is
  - Which URL to access the demo app
  - Link of the video demo (to be provided later once the implementation is finished)
  - What tech stacks are used
  - Instructions on how to run the project locally or in development mode
  - Instructions on how to deploy the app live
- Any updates on the architecture, plans, workflows, or tech stacks should update/amend the `README.md`.
- The `README.md` must include a **Project Deliverables** section for hackathon judges, containing links to external or internal sources that judges can view.
- Consult me first or ask me questions if you are about to execute complicated tasks.</content>

# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.

- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.

data.content:
# Create Plan

Follow this structured workflow to produce a high-quality, actionable plan.

## Step 1 — Gather Requirements

Ask the user clarifying questions to fully understand the task:
- What is the goal and expected outcome?
- Are there constraints, preferences, or non-goals?
- Which parts of the codebase are likely involved?
- Any related issues or requirement documents?

Do not proceed until you have enough context to scope the work, be critical of vague intent or requirements.

## Step 2 — Code Search via Sub-Agent

Spawn a `spawn_subagent` of type `"explore"` to research the codebase. The sub-agent should:
- Locate relevant files, symbols, and patterns related to the task
- Identify existing utilities or abstractions that should be reused
- Identify existing design patterns
- Surface any constraints or conventions (e.g. patterns in similar files)

Use the sub-agent's findings to ground your plan in the actual code.

## Step 3 — Clarify Design Intention

Based on the requirements and code research:
- Always confirm your understanding of the intended design with the user
- Raise any open questions or trade-offs that need a decision
- Adjust scope if the code research revealed complexity or simplifications

Do not begin writing the plan document until design intent is confirmed.

## Step 4 — Write the Plan File

Write a structured plan to a markdown file (e.g. `{short-plan-name}-plan.md`). The plan must NOT go into low-level code detail — focus on *what* needs to happen and *why*.

The plan file must include:

### Top-Level Overview
A concise summary of the goal, scope, and approach.

### Sub-Tasks
Break the work into sub-tasks. Each sub-task must have:
- **Intent** — what this sub-task achieves and why
- **Expected Outcomes** — observable results when this sub-task is complete
- **Todo List** — ordered, specific steps to achieve the outcome
- **Relevant Context** — pointers to relevant files, symbols, or patterns
- **Status** — `[ ] pending` (updated to `[x] done` after completion)

Design each sub-task to be processed independently, one at a time, so changes stay focused and reviewable.

## Step 5 — Plan Validation

Before moving to implementation, ensure that the user has fully read the plan. Always ask the user targeted questions to verify the plan is correct and complete:
- Does this plan capture the full scope of the task?
- Are the sub-task boundaries and ordering correct?
- Is any context missing that would be needed during implementation?

Use Mermaid diagrams in chat responses where they clarify architecture or workflow, but do not place Mermaid diagrams directly in the plan file. Avoid double quotes and parentheses inside square brackets in Mermaid syntax.

Refine the plan file based on the user's answers.

## Step 6 — Implementation

Only after the user confirms the plan, recommend implementation by calling the `switch_mode` tool to `agent`.

When explaining how to implement the plan in agent mode:
- Using the `start_subtask` tool, create a new task for each subtask in the <plan-file>.
- In the prompt for the subtask make sure it reads the plan-file to gain the full context around the task.
- After each sub task is complete update the task status in the <plan-file>
- Add any context needed for the next subtask in the <plan-file>
- Wait for the user to check and ok the changes before moving on to the next subtask.

## Reminders

- Ask questions always using the "ask_followup_question" tool
- Never include information without evidence
- Don't include time estimates
Let me research the current codebase to understand what's already built before scoping the plan.

<task_result>
Perfect! Now let me provide a comprehensive summary of the codebase:

---

## COMPREHENSIVE CODEBASE SUMMARY: Standup Sync

### **1. PROJECT STRUCTURE (Top-Level)**

```
ibm-hackathon/
├── backend/                    # Python FastAPI backend
├── frontend/                   # Single-page HTML UI
├── prompts/                    # LLM prompt templates
├── plan/                       # Architecture documentation
├── deliverables/               # Hackathon submission artifacts
├── bob_sessions/               # Bob session screenshots
├── tests/                      # Test files
├── .env.example                # Environment template
├── requirements.txt            # Python dependencies
├── README.md                   # Project overview
└── venv/                       # Virtual environment
```

---

### **2. FRONTEND UI CODE**

**File:** `frontend/index.html` (Single-page application)

**Structure:**
- **Input form** (lines 88-118):
  - Repository path/URL input
  - Date range selector ("Last 24h", "Last 48h", "Last 7 days", "Last 30 days")
  - Optional "until" date picker
  - Generate button

- **Results section** (lines 121-166):
  - **Before/After panel**: Raw git log vs. generated summary (side-by-side)
  - **Blockers section**: Displays flagged issues (repeated files, reverts, WIP patterns)
  - **Output tabs**: Slack, Email, Standup formats with copy-to-clipboard buttons

**Frontend JavaScript (lines 170-321):**
- **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** stream handler (lines 248-292):
  - Handles `progress` events → updates step indicators
  - Handles `raw_log` events → displays raw commits immediately
  - Handles `result` events → populates all output tabs
  - Handles `error` events → displays error messages
  
- **Step tracking** (lines 173-175):
  - Maps backend steps: `clone` → `extract` → `filter` → `llm` → `render`
  - UI shows progress badges: ① Clone repo → ② Extract commits → ③ Filter noise → ④ Analyse diffs → ⑤ Render output

- **Data rendering** (lines 211-239):
  - `currentFormats` global stores `{ slack, email, standup }` strings
  - Renders blockers with conditional text based on `reason`: "repeated_changes" or "possible_struggle"
  - Displays commit count in status message

- **Tab switching** (lines 305-312): Toggle between format outputs

---

### **3. BACKEND API & ENDPOINTS**

**Main file:** `backend/main.py`

**Entry point:** `POST /api/generate`
- **Request body:**
  ```json
  {
    "repo": "https://github.com/org/repo or /local/path",
    "since": "24 hours ago",
    "until": null  // optional
  }
  ```

- **Response:** Server-Sent Events stream with 4 event types:
  1. `progress`: `{step, message}`
  2. `raw_log`: `{lines: [string]}`
  3. `result`: `{summary, formats: {slack, email, standup}}`
  4. `error`: `{detail}`

---

### **4. BACKEND PIPELINE & DATA FLOW**

**Pipeline steps** (backend/main.py lines 49-108):

1. **Extract commits** (`git_extractor.py` → `extract_commits()`)
   - Clones repo (if URL) into temp dir or uses local path
   - Runs: `git log --no-merges -p --format=COMMIT_START|%H|%an|%ai|%s`
   - Returns: `[{hash, author, timestamp, message, diff, files_changed}]`

2. **Filter noise** (`noise_filter.py` → `filter_commits()`)
   - Drops commits touching only lockfiles/generated files (package-lock.json, yarn.lock, dist/, etc.)
   - Drops whitespace-only diffs
   - Returns: Filtered subset

3. **Analyze diffs (LLM)** (`diff_analyzer.py` → `analyze_commits()`)
   - Batches commits (10 per call) for concurrent LLM processing
   - Sends to LLM with prompt template: "What changed and why in one sentence?"
   - Adds `summary` field to each commit
   - Returns: Same commits with `summary` enriched

4. **Group commits** (`grouper.py` → `group_commits()`)
   - Groups by most common top-level directory touched
   - Collects author names per group
   - Returns: `[{theme, commits, authors}]` sorted by commit count (desc)

5. **Detect blockers** (`blocker_detector.py` → `detect_blockers()`)
   - Flags files appearing in 3+ commits: `{target, reason: "repeated_changes"}`
   - Flags commits with "revert", "undo", "wip", "fix fix" patterns: `{target: hash, reason: "possible_struggle", message}`
   - Returns: List of blocker objects

6. **Build summary** (`summarizer.py` → `build_summary()`)
   - Canonical object consumed by all renderers:
     ```python
     {
       "repo": str,
       "range": {"since": str, "until": str},
       "groups": [{theme, commits: [{hash, author, message, summary, files_changed}], authors}],
       "blockers": [{target, reason, message?}],
       "raw_log": [string]  # formatted for UI
     }
     ```

7. **Render outputs** (three pure functions):
   - `slack_renderer.py`: Emoji-friendly format with blockers section
   - `email_renderer.py`: Plain-text email with subject + formal tone
   - `standup_renderer.py`: Grouped by author, includes per-person blockers

---

### **5. DATA RETURNED TO FRONTEND**

**API Response shape** (`/api/generate` → `result` event):

```json
{
  "summary": {
    "repo": "https://github.com/user/repo",
    "range": {
      "since": "24 hours ago",
      "until": "2025-01-15T14:30:00Z"
    },
    "groups": [
      {
        "theme": "src",
        "commits": [
          {
            "hash": "abc1234def567...",
            "author": "Alice",
            "timestamp": "2025-01-15T10:30:00Z",
            "message": "fix: auth token expiry",
            "summary": "Fixed auth token refresh logic to handle expiry gracefully",
            "diff": "--- a/src/auth.ts\n+++ b/src/auth.ts\n@@ -10,5 +10,6 @@\n...",
            "files_changed": ["src/auth.ts", "src/types.ts"]
          }
        ],
        "authors": ["Alice"]
      }
    ],
    "blockers": [
      {
        "target": "src/utils/logger.ts",
        "reason": "repeated_changes",
        "message": null
      },
      {
        "target": "abc1234def567...",
        "reason": "possible_struggle",
        "message": "WIP: debugging logger bug"
      }
    ],
    "raw_log": [
      "abc1234 Alice — fix: auth token expiry",
      "def5678 Bob — refactor: logger module"
    ]
  },
  "formats": {
    "slack": "*📋 Standup Sync — `https://github.com/user/repo`*\n_24 hours ago  →  2025-01-15T14:30:00Z_\n\n*src* _(by Alice)_\n  • Fixed auth token refresh logic...",
    "email": "Subject: Project Update — https://github.com/user/repo\nPeriod: 24 hours ago to 2025-01-15T14:30:00Z\n\nHi team,\n\nHere's a summary of recent progress:\n\n[SRC] — Alice\n  - Fixed auth token refresh logic...",
    "standup": "STANDUP NOTES — https://github.com/user/repo\n24 hours ago → 2025-01-15T14:30:00Z\n\n👤 Alice\n  What I did:\n    • [src] Fixed auth token refresh logic...\n  Possible blockers:\n    ⚠️  Fixed auth token refresh logic..."
  }
}
```

---

### **6. FRONTEND RENDERING LOGIC**

**How frontend processes data** (index.html, lines 211-239):

1. **`showResult(data)` function:**
   - Extracts `data.formats` into global `currentFormats`
   - Renders raw log: `raw_log` array joined with `\n` → `#raw-log` element
   - Renders summary preview from slack format → `#summary-preview`
   - Processes blockers:
     ```javascript
     if (b.reason === 'repeated_changes')
       → "{{file}} was modified in 3+ commits — possible rework or ongoing issue."
     else if (b.reason === 'possible_struggle')
       → "Commit {{hash[:7]}} flagged: '{{message}}' — possible struggle."
     ```
   - Sets tab content: `#output-slack`, `#output-email`, `#output-standup`

2. **Stream event handling:**
   - `progress`: Shows spinner + message, updates step badges
   - `raw_log`: Immediate display of raw commits before LLM finishes (lines 276-280)
   - `result`: Populates all tabs and blockers list
   - `error`: Displays error in red text

3. **Copy-to-clipboard:** `copyTab(format)` → `navigator.clipboard.writeText(currentFormats[format])`

---

### **7. KEY FILES & THEIR ROLES**

| File | Purpose | Key Output |
|------|---------|-----------|
| `backend/git_extractor.py` | Extract commits from git | `[{hash, author, timestamp, message, diff, files_changed}]` |
| `backend/noise_filter.py` | Filter low-signal commits | Same shape, filtered |
| `backend/diff_analyzer.py` | LLM-based diff summarization | Commits + `summary` field |
| `backend/grouper.py` | Group by directory/author | `[{theme, commits, authors}]` |
| `backend/blocker_detector.py` | Detect struggle patterns | `[{target, reason, message?}]` |
| `backend/summarizer.py` | Assemble canonical object | Final summary dict |
| `backend/renderers/slack_renderer.py` | Format for Slack | Plain text with Slack markup |
| `backend/renderers/email_renderer.py` | Format for email | Plain text with subject line |
| `backend/renderers/standup_renderer.py` | Format by author | Author-grouped standup notes |
| `backend/llm_client.py` | LLM abstraction layer | Supports IBM watsonx + Anthropic |
| `backend/main.py` | FastAPI orchestration | SSE streaming response |
| `frontend/index.html` | Single-page UI | Input form + results display |

---

### **8. LLM INTEGRATION**

**File:** `backend/llm_client.py`

- **Providers:** IBM watsonx (default) or Anthropic Claude
- **Model:** `mistralai/mistral-small-3-1-24b-instruct-2503` (watsonx) or `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` (Anthropic)
- **Prompt:** Reads from `prompts/diff_analysis.txt` (template)
- **Usage:** Batches commits (10 per call), concurrent calls (3 workers max)
- **Response parse:** Numbered list `1. xxx` → extract summaries

---

### **SUMMARY OF DATA FLOW**

```
Frontend Input (repo, since, until)
           ↓
POST /api/generate (SSE stream)
           ↓
[Git Extract] → raw_commits
           ↓
[Noise Filter] → filtered_commits
           ↓
[LLM Diff Analysis] → analyzed_commits (+ summary)
           ↓
[Grouping] → groups (by theme)
           ↓
[Blocker Detection] → blockers
           ↓
[Summary Builder] → canonical summary object
           ↓
[Three Renderers] → formats: {slack, email, standup}
           ↓
SSE Event: result {summary, formats}
           ↓
Frontend JS → Populate tabs + render blockers
```
</task_result>

You are a fast codebase exploration agent. Your only job is to find and return relevant code context.

2 | diff_analyzer.py
3 | 
4 | Sends filtered commits to the LLM in batches, concurrently.
5 | Returns each commit enriched with a plain-English summary sentence.
6 | """
7 | 
8 | import re
9 | from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
10 | from pathlib import Path
11 | from backend.llm_client import generate
12 | 
13 | _PROMPT_PATH = Path(__file__).parent.parent / "prompts" / "diff_analysis.txt"
14 | _BATCH_SIZE = 10   # commits per LLM call
15 | _MAX_WORKERS = 3   # concurrent LLM calls
16 | _DIFF_LIMIT = 4000 # chars per diff — enough to fit most real diffs in full
17 | 
18 | 
19 | def analyze_commits(commits: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
20 |     """
21 |     Enrich each commit with a plain-English 'summary' field.
22 |     Batches are sent to the LLM concurrently for speed.
23 | 
24 |     Args:
25 |         commits: Filtered commit list from noise_filter.filter_commits().
26 | 
27 |     Returns:
28 |         Same list with 'summary' field added to each commit dict.
29 |     """
30 |     if not commits:
31 |         return []
32 | 
33 |     prompt_template = _PROMPT_PATH.read_text()
34 |     batches = _batch(commits, _BATCH_SIZE)
35 | 
36 |     # Run all batches concurrently, preserve original order
37 |     results_by_index: dict[int, list[dict]] = {}
38 |     with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=_MAX_WORKERS) as executor:
39 |         futures = {
40 |             executor.submit(_analyze_batch, batch, prompt_template): i
41 |             for i, batch in enumerate(batches)
42 |         }
43 |         for future in as_completed(futures):
44 |             i = futures[future]
45 |             results_by_index[i] = future.result()
46 | 
47 |     # Flatten back in original order
48 |     results = []
49 |     for i in range(len(batches)):
50 |         results.extend(results_by_index[i])
51 |     return results
52 | 
53 | 
54 | def _batch(items: list, size: int) -> list[list]:
55 |     """Split a list into chunks of at most `size` items."""
56 |     return [items[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(items), size)]
57 | 
58 | 
59 | def _analyze_batch(batch: list[dict], prompt_template: str) -> list[dict]:
60 |     """Send one batch of commits to the LLM, return enriched commit dicts."""
61 |     commits_text = ""
62 |     for i, commit in enumerate(batch, 1):
63 |         diff_snippet = commit["diff"][:_DIFF_LIMIT] if commit["diff"] else "(no diff)"
64 |         commits_text += (
65 |             f"\n---\nCommit {i}\n"
66 |             f"Message: {commit['message']}\n"
67 |             f"Files: {', '.join(commit['files_changed']) or 'unknown'}\n"
68 |             f"Diff:\n{diff_snippet}\n"
69 |         )
70 | 
71 |     prompt = prompt_template.replace("{{COMMITS}}", commits_text).replace(
72 |         "{{COUNT}}", str(len(batch))
73 |     )
74 | 
75 |     raw_response = generate(prompt)
76 |     summaries = _parse_summaries(raw_response, len(batch))
77 |     return [{**commit, "summary": summary} for commit, summary in zip(batch, summaries)]
78 | 
79 | 
80 | def _parse_summaries(response: str, expected_count: int) -> list[str]:
81 |     """
82 |     Parse numbered list from LLM response.
83 |     Falls back gracefully if the model doesn't follow the format.
84 |     """
85 |     lines = [l.strip() for l in response.splitlines() if l.strip()]
86 |     # Try to match lines starting with "1.", "2.", etc.
87 |     numbered = [re.sub(r"^\d+\.\s*", "", l) for l in lines if re.match(r"^\d+\.", l)]
88 |     if len(numbered) == expected_count:
89 |         return numbered
90 |     # Fallback: return raw lines, padded/trimmed to expected count
91 |     padded = (lines + ["(summary unavailable)"] * expected_count)[:expected_count]
92 |     return padded

38 |         if repo.startswith("http://") or repo.startswith("https://") or repo.startswith("git@"):
39 |             tmp_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="standup_sync_")
40 |             _run(["git", "clone", "--bare", "--filter=blob:none", "--depth=200", repo, tmp_dir])
41 |             repo_path = tmp_dir
42 |         else:
43 |             repo_path = repo
44 | 
45 |         _verify_repo(repo_path)
46 | 
47 |         cmd = [
48 |             "git", "-C", repo_path,
49 |             "log",
50 |             "--no-merges",
51 |             f"--since={since}",
52 |             "-p",
53 |             "--no-color",
54 |             "--format=COMMIT_START|%H|%an|%ai|%s",
55 |         ]
56 |         if until:
57 |             cmd.append(f"--until={until}")
58 | 
59 |         raw = _run(cmd)
60 |         return _parse_log(raw)
61 | 
62 |     finally:
63 |         if tmp_dir:
64 |             shutil.rmtree(tmp_dir, ignore_errors=True)
65 | 
66 | 
67 | def _verify_repo(path: str) -> None:
68 |     result = subprocess.run(
69 |         ["git", "-C", path, "rev-parse", "--git-dir"],
70 |         capture_output=True, text=True
71 |     )
72 |     if result.returncode != 0:
73 |         raise ValueError(f"Not a valid git repository: {path}")
74 | 
75 | 
76 | def _run(cmd: list[str]) -> str:
77 |     result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)
78 |     if result.returncode != 0:
79 |         raise RuntimeError(f"git command failed: {' '.join(cmd)}\n{result.stderr}")
80 |     return result.stdout
81 | 
82 | 
83 | def _parse_log(raw: str) -> list[dict]:
84 |     """Split raw git log -p output into structured commit objects."""
85 |     commits = []
86 |     # Split on our custom separator line
87 |     blocks = re.split(r"(?=COMMIT_START\|)", raw)
88 | 
89 |     for block in blocks:
90 |         block = block.strip()
91 |         if not block.startswith("COMMIT_START|"):
92 |             continue
93 | 
94 |         lines = block.splitlines()
95 |         header = lines[0]
96 |         parts = header.split("|", 4)
97 |         if len(parts) < 5:
98 |             continue
99 | 
100 |         _, hash_, author, timestamp, message = parts
101 |         diff = "\n".join(lines[1:]).strip()
102 | 
103 |         # Collect touched file names from diff headers
104 |         files_changed = re.findall(r"^diff --git a/(.+?) b/", diff, re.MULTILINE)
105 | 
106 |         commits.append({
107 |             "hash": hash_.strip(),
108 |             "author": author.strip(),
109 |             "timestamp": timestamp.strip(),
110 |             "message": message.strip(),
111 |             "diff": diff,
112 |             "files_changed": files_changed,
113 |         })
114 | 
115 |     return commits
116 |

1 | """
2 | noise_filter.py
3 | 
4 | Pure function — no LLM calls.
5 | Drops commits that carry no meaningful signal:
6 |   - all changed files are generated/lock files
7 |   - the diff is whitespace/formatting only
8 | """
9 | 
10 | import re
11 | 
12 | # Patterns for generated or lock files — extend as needed
13 | GENERATED_FILE_PATTERNS = [
14 |     r"package-lock\.json$",
15 |     r"yarn\.lock$",
16 |     r"pnpm-lock\.yaml$",
17 |     r"composer\.lock$",
18 |     r"Pipfile\.lock$",
19 |     r"poetry\.lock$",
20 |     r"\.min\.js$",
21 |     r"\.min\.css$",
22 |     r"dist/",
23 |     r"build/",
24 |     r"\.next/",
25 |     r"__pycache__/",
26 |     r"\.pyc$",
27 |     r"coverage/",
28 |     r"\.map$",
29 | ]
30 | 
31 | _GENERATED_RE = re.compile("|".join(GENERATED_FILE_PATTERNS))
32 | 
33 | 
34 | def filter_commits(commits: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
35 |     """
36 |     Remove low-signal commits from a list.
37 | 
38 |     Args:
39 |         commits: Raw commit list from git_extractor.extract_commits().
40 | 
41 |     Returns:
42 |         Filtered list — same shape, subset of input.
43 |     """
44 |     return [c for c in commits if _is_meaningful(c)]
45 | 
46 | 
47 | def _is_meaningful(commit: dict) -> bool:
48 |     files = commit.get("files_changed", [])
49 |     diff = commit.get("diff", "")
50 | 
51 |     # Keep commits that touch at least one non-generated file
52 |     real_files = [f for f in files if not _GENERATED_RE.search(f)]
53 |     if files and not real_files:
54 |         return False
55 | 
56 |     # Drop whitespace/formatting-only diffs
57 |     if diff and _is_whitespace_only(diff):
58 |         return False
59 | 
60 |     return True
61 | 
62 | 
63 | def _is_whitespace_only(diff: str) -> bool:
64 |     """
65 |     Returns True if every changed line (+ or - prefix) differs only in whitespace.
66 |     """
67 |     added = []
68 |     removed = []
69 | 
70 |     for line in diff.splitlines():
71 |         if line.startswith("+") and not line.startswith("+++"):
72 |             added.append(line[1:])
73 |         elif line.startswith("-") and not line.startswith("---"):
74 |             removed.append(line[1:])
75 | 
76 |     if not added and not removed:
77 |         return True
78 | 
79 |     all_lines = added + removed
80 |     return all(line.strip() == "" for line in all_lines)

1 | """
2 | blocker_detector.py
3 | 
4 | Pure function — no LLM calls.
5 | Flags patterns that suggest a developer is struggling:
6 |   - Same file touched in 3+ commits within the window
7 |   - Commit message contains "revert", "undo", "wip", or "fix fix"
8 | """
9 | 
10 | import re
11 | from collections import Counter
12 | 
13 | _STRUGGLE_RE = re.compile(r"\b(revert|undo|wip|fix fix)\b", re.IGNORECASE)
14 | _REPEATED_FILE_THRESHOLD = 3
15 | 
16 | 
17 | def detect_blockers(commits: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
18 |     """
19 |     Scan all commits and return a list of blocker signals.
20 | 
21 |     Args:
22 |         commits: Full analyzed commit list (pre-grouping is fine).
23 | 
24 |     Returns:
25 |         List of blocker dicts: {target, reason}
26 |         - target: the file path or commit hash that triggered the flag
27 |         - reason: "repeated_changes" | "possible_struggle"
28 |     """
29 |     blockers = []
30 |     blockers.extend(_find_repeated_files(commits))
31 |     blockers.extend(_find_struggle_messages(commits))
32 |     return blockers
33 | 
34 | 
35 | def _find_repeated_files(commits: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
36 |     """Flag files that appear in 3 or more commits."""
37 |     file_counts: Counter = Counter()
38 |     for commit in commits:
39 |         for f in commit.get("files_changed", []):
40 |             file_counts[f] += 1
41 | 
42 |     return [
43 |         {"target": file, "reason": "repeated_changes"}
44 |         for file, count in file_counts.items()
45 |         if count >= _REPEATED_FILE_THRESHOLD
46 |     ]
47 | 
48 | 
49 | def _find_struggle_messages(commits: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
50 |     """Flag commits whose message matches struggle keywords."""
51 |     blockers = []
52 |     for commit in commits:
53 |         if _STRUGGLE_RE.search(commit.get("message", "")):
54 |             blockers.append({
55 |                 "target": commit["hash"],
56 |                 "reason": "possible_struggle",
57 |                 "message": commit["message"],
58 |             })
59 |     return blockers

Here's what I found and my proposed design. Let me confirm before writing the plan:

---

## What the data currently has

The `diff` field on each commit already contains the raw `git log -p` patch output. From it we can deterministically parse (no LLM):

- **File added** — `diff --git a/foo b/foo` where the `---` line is `--- /dev/null`
- **File deleted** — `+++` line is `+++ /dev/null`
- **File modified** — everything else
- **Lines added** — count of `+` lines (excluding the `+++ b/...` header)
- **Lines deleted** — count of `-` lines (excluding the `--- a/...` header)
- **Lines updated** isn't a native git concept — it's typically approximated as `min(lines_added, lines_deleted)`, with the remainder being pure additions/deletions

## Proposed approach

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[git_extractor.py\nparses diff] --> B[NEW: parse_diff_stats\nin git_extractor.py]
    B --> C[Each commit gets\nfiles_added, files_deleted,\nfiles_modified, lines_added,\nlines_deleted]
    C --> D[summarizer.py\naggregates per-author]
    D --> E[summary object gets\nauthor_stats dict]
    E --> F[frontend renders\nDeveloper Stats table]
```

**3 changes needed:**

1. **`backend/git_extractor.py`** — add a `_parse_diff_stats(diff)` pure function that counts file add/delete/modify and lines +/-. Call it in `_parse_log()` to enrich each commit with `files_added`, `files_deleted`, `files_modified`, `lines_added`, `lines_deleted`.

2. **`backend/summarizer.py`** — aggregate those per-commit stats by author into an `author_stats` dict: `{ "Alice": { files_added, files_deleted, files_modified, lines_added, lines_deleted, commit_count } }`. Include it in the returned summary object.

3. **`frontend/index.html`** — add a new "Developer Stats" card in the results section that renders the `author_stats` as a table: one row per developer, columns for commits, files added/deleted/modified, lines added/deleted.

A few quick design questions before I write the plan:

1. For "lines updated" — git doesn't track this natively. The closest approximation is `min(lines_added, lines_deleted)` per hunk (a changed block). Should I use that approximation, or just show "lines added" and "lines deleted" without a separate "updated" column?

2. Where in the results page should the Developer Stats table appear? Options: (a) as a new card above the Before/After panel, (b) between Before/After and Blockers, or (c) as a new tab alongside Slack/Email/Standup in the Output Formats card?

3. Should the stats table be sorted by number of commits (most active developer first), or alphabetically by name?

# Developer Stats UI — Plan ## Top-Level Overview Add a per-developer stats table to the Standup Sync UI that shows — for the given repo and date range — each developer who pushed commits, with columns for: commits, files added, files deleted, files modified, lines added, lines deleted, and lines updated (approximated as per-hunk minimum of added/deleted lines in each diff hunk). The stats table appears **above** the existing "Before vs. After" card in the results section. It is sortable: default sort is by commit count (descending), with a toggle to sort alphabetically by developer name. All stat computation is deterministic (no LLM calls). The `diff` field already present on each commit contains the full `git log -p` patch — we parse it in the backend and aggregate by author, then pass the aggregated data to the frontend in the existing `result` SSE event payload. --- ## Sub-Tasks --- ### Sub-Task 1 — Parse diff stats per commit in `git_extractor.py` **Status:** `[ ] pending` **Intent** Add a pure function `_parse_diff_stats(diff: str) -> dict` to [`backend/git_extractor.py`](../backend/git_extractor.py) that reads the raw patch text of a single commit and returns file-level and line-level counts. Call it inside `_parse_log()` so every commit dict gets the new fields. **Expected Outcomes** - Every commit dict returned by `extract_commits()` has five new integer fields: `files_added`, `files_deleted`, `files_modified`, `lines_added`, `lines_deleted`, `lines_updated`. - The function is a pure, standalone function with no side effects and no LLM calls. - Existing fields (`hash`, `author`, `timestamp`, `message`, `diff`, `files_changed`) are unchanged. **Todo List** 1. In `_parse_diff_stats(diff)`: - Split diff on `diff --git` boundaries to get one block per file. - For each block: classify as **added** if `--- /dev/null` is present, **deleted** if `+++ /dev/null` is present, else **modified**. - Count `lines_added`: lines beginning with `+` that are NOT the `+++ b/...` header. - Count `lines_deleted`: lines beginning with `-` that are NOT the `--- a/...` header. - Compute `lines_updated`: iterate over diff hunks (sections between `@@` markers); for each hunk, `min(hunk_plus_count, hunk_minus_count)` — sum these across all hunks. This is the per-hunk approximation of "updated" lines. 2. In `_parse_log()`, after building the commit dict, call `_parse_diff_stats(diff)` and merge the result into the commit dict. **Relevant Context** - File: [`backend/git_extractor.py`](../backend/git_extractor.py) - The `diff` variable is already populated at line 101 as `"\n".join(lines[1:]).strip()`. - The commit dict is assembled at lines 106–113. --- ### Sub-Task 2 — Aggregate per-author stats in `summarizer.py` **Status:** `[ ] pending` **Intent** In [`backend/summarizer.py`](../backend/summarizer.py), aggregate the per-commit stat fields across all commits for each author and add an `author_stats` key to the returned summary object. This is consumed by the frontend to render the table. **Expected Outcomes** - The summary object returned by `build_summary()` includes a new `author_stats` key. - Shape: ```json { "author_stats": { "Alice": { "commits": 3, "files_added": 5, "files_deleted": 1, "files_modified": 12, "lines_added": 220, "lines_deleted": 45, "lines_updated": 30 } } } ``` - Aggregation uses `raw_commits` (the full unfiltered list) so noise-filtered commits still appear in stats. Wait — reconsider: use the **filtered** commits passed through the pipeline (the same commits that reach analysis), since those represent real signal. The `raw_commits` parameter is already the post-filter list at the call site in `main.py`. **Todo List** 1. In `build_summary()`, add an aggregation loop over `raw_commits`. 2. For each commit, accumulate each of the 6 stat fields under the commit's `author` key. Initialize missing authors on first encounter. 3. Add `"author_stats": author_stats` to the returned dict. **Relevant Context** - File: [`backend/summarizer.py`](../backend/summarizer.py) - `raw_commits` is already passed in — it is the filtered commit list from `main.py` (see call site in `backend/main.py`). - The 6 new fields (`files_added`, `files_deleted`, `files_modified`, `lines_added`, `lines_deleted`, `lines_updated`) are added in Sub-Task 1. --- ### Sub-Task 3 — Render Developer Stats table in `frontend/index.html` **Status:** `[ ] pending` **Intent** Add a new "Developer Stats" results card to the frontend that renders `author_stats` as a sortable table. The card is placed **above** the existing "Before vs. After" card. Default sort: by commit count descending. Secondary sort: alphabetical by name (toggled via a sort button). **Expected Outcomes** - A new card appears in the results section, above "Before vs. After", once results arrive. - Table columns: Developer | Commits | Files Added | Files Deleted | Files Modified | Lines Added | Lines Deleted | Lines Updated. - Default sort: highest commit count first. - A "Sort A→Z" button (toggles to "Sort by Commits") re-sorts the table rows in place without re-fetching. - Numbers are right-aligned in the table; developer name is left-aligned. - Added/deleted columns use subtle green/red coloring to make the data scannable at a glance. - If `author_stats` is empty or missing, the card is hidden (same pattern as the blockers card). **Todo List** 1. Add CSS for the stats table: `.stats-table` — full width, clean borders, right-aligned number cells, color classes `.added` (green), `.deleted` (red), `.updated` (muted blue). 2. Add the HTML card skeleton above the "Before vs. After" card inside `#results`: ```html

👥 Developer Stats

...
``` 3. In `showResult(data)`, call a new `renderDevStats(data.summary.author_stats)` function. 4. `renderDevStats(authorStats)`: - Build a rows array from `Object.entries(authorStats)`. - Sort by commit count descending by default. - Render `` elements into `#dev-stats-table tbody`. - Show/hide the section card. 5. Add sort toggle button logic: clicking "Sort A→Z" re-sorts rows alphabetically and relabels the button to "Sort by Commits"; clicking again reverts. **Relevant Context** - File: [`frontend/index.html`](../frontend/index.html) - The "Before vs. After" card starts at line 124. The new card goes before it, inside `#results` (line 121). - Pattern for show/hide: `blockersSection.classList.remove('hidden')` — same approach. - `showResult(data)` is at line 211 — add the `renderDevStats` call there. --- ## Implementation Notes - `lines_updated` approximation: for each `@@` hunk in the diff, `lines_updated += min(plus_lines_in_hunk, minus_lines_in_hunk)`. This avoids double-counting and represents lines that were truly changed in place rather than purely added or removed. - Sub-Tasks must be done in order: 1 → 2 → 3 (each feeds the next). - No new dependencies, no new endpoints, no schema changes to the SSE event format beyond adding `author_stats` to the existing `summary` object.

    until: Optional[str] = None,
) -> list[dict]:

        RuntimeError: if git subprocess fails.

            "log",
            "--no-merges",

            "-p",
            "--no-color",

        ]

"""
summarizer.py

Assembles the final summary object from grouped commits and blockers.
This is the single source of truth that all format renderers consume.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timezone


def build_summary(
    repo: str,
    since: str,
    until: str | None,
    groups: list[dict],
    blockers: list[dict],
    raw_commits: list[dict],
) -> dict:
    """
    Assemble the canonical summary object.

    Returns:
        {
            repo, range: {since, until},
            groups: [{theme, commits, authors}],
            blockers: [{target, reason}],
            raw_log: [raw commit messages for before/after view]
        }
    """
    until_str = until or datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

    raw_log = [
        f"{c['hash'][:7]} {c['author']} — {c['message']}"
        for c in raw_commits
    ]

    # Aggregate per-commit stats by author
    _STAT_KEYS = ("files_added", "files_deleted", "files_modified",
                  "lines_added", "lines_deleted", "lines_updated")
    author_stats: dict[str, dict] = {}
    for c in raw_commits:
        author = c["author"]
        if author not in author_stats:
            author_stats[author] = {"commits": 0, **{k: 0 for k in _STAT_KEYS}}
        author_stats[author]["commits"] += 1
        for k in _STAT_KEYS:
            author_stats[author][k] += c.get(k, 0)

    return {
        "repo": repo,
        "range": {
            "since": since,
            "until": until_str,
        },
        "groups": groups,
        "blockers": blockers,
        "raw_log": raw_log,
        "author_stats": author_stats,
    }

**No — the stats are not from the LLM summary.** They are parsed directly from the raw `git diff` output (`git log -p`), which is already being fetched. Specifically:

- **Files added/deleted/modified** → detected from `--- /dev/null` and `+++ /dev/null` markers in each file block of the patch
- **Lines added/deleted** → counted from `+`/`-` prefixed lines in the patch hunks
- **Lines updated** → computed as `Σ min(plus_lines, minus_lines)` per hunk — pure arithmetic, no LLM

The LLM is only used for the plain-English per-commit "what changed and why" description. The stats are 100% deterministic parsing of the diff text that git already provides.

def _parse_diff_stats(diff: str) -> dict:
    """
    Parse a raw git diff patch and return file-level and line-level counts.

    File classification per file block:
      - added:    source is /dev/null  (--- /dev/null)
      - deleted:  dest   is /dev/null  (+++ /dev/null)
      - modified: everything else

    lines_added:   count of '+' lines excluding '+++ b/...' headers
    lines_deleted: count of '-' lines excluding '--- a/...' headers
    lines_updated: per-hunk min(plus_lines, minus_lines) summed across all hunks
                   — approximates lines changed in-place rather than purely added/removed

    Returns:
        {files_added, files_deleted, files_modified, lines_added, lines_deleted, lines_updated}
    """
    files_added = files_deleted = files_modified = 0
    total_lines_added = total_lines_deleted = total_lines_updated = 0

    # Split into per-file blocks on "diff --git" boundaries
    file_blocks = re.split(r"(?=^diff --git )", diff, flags=re.MULTILINE)

    for block in file_blocks:

"""

Assembles the final summary object from grouped commits and blockers.
This is the single source of truth that all format renderers consume.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timezone


def build_summary(
    repo: str,
    since: str,
    until: str | None,
    groups: list[dict],
    blockers: list[dict],
    raw_commits: list[dict],
) -> dict:
    """
    Assemble the canonical summary object.

    Returns:
        {
            repo, range: {since, until},
            groups: [{theme, commits, authors}],
            blockers: [{target, reason}],
            raw_log: [raw commit messages for before/after view]
        }
    """
    until_str = until or datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

    raw_log = [
        f"{c['hash'][:7]} {c['author']} — {c['message']}"
        for c in raw_commits
    ]

    # Aggregate per-commit stats by author
    _STAT_KEYS = ("files_added", "files_deleted", "files_modified",
                  "lines_added", "lines_deleted", "lines_updated")
    author_stats: dict[str, dict] = {}
    for c in raw_commits:
        author = c["author"]
        if author not in author_stats:
            author_stats[author] = {"commits": 0, **{k: 0 for k in _STAT_KEYS}}
        author_stats[author]["commits"] += 1
        for k in _STAT_KEYS:
            author_stats[author][k] += c.get(k, 0)

    return {
        "repo": repo,
        "range": {
            "since": since,
            "until": until_str,
        },
        "groups": groups,
        "blockers": blockers,
        "raw_log": raw_log,
        "author_stats": author_stats,
    }

data.content:
All re-applied and validated. To directly answer your question:

**No — the stats don't touch the LLM at all.** Everything comes from parsing the raw `git diff` text that `git log -p` already produces:

| Stat | Source |
|---|---|
| Files added/deleted/modified | `--- /dev/null` / `+++ /dev/null` markers in each file block |
| Lines added | Count of `+` prefixed lines per hunk |
| Lines deleted | Count of `-` prefixed lines per hunk |
| Lines updated | `Σ min(+lines, -lines)` per hunk — lines that changed in-place |

The LLM is only called once, in [`diff_analyzer.py`](backend/diff_analyzer.py), to generate the plain-English "what changed and why" sentence per commit. The stats table is fully deterministic and free.

def generate(prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 200) -> str:
    """
    Send a prompt to the configured LLM and return the response text.

    Args:

        max_tokens: Maximum tokens to generate. Defaults to 200 (enough for

    if _PROVIDER == "anthropic":

        response = client.messages.create(

            max_tokens=max_tokens,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],

data.content: **Step 3 — add a `client_renderer.py`** that generates the client-facing narrative and renders all three format variants from it. A single LLM call produces the narrative; three pure formatting functions wrap it differently for Slack, Email, and Standup:

arguments.content:
"""
client_renderer.py

Generates client-facing (non-technical) versions of all three output formats.
One LLM call produces a plain-English benefit narrative; three pure functions
then wrap it into the appropriate format shape.

The client-facing tone:
  - No file names, packages, or code references
  - Focuses on user benefit: what changed, why it matters, what improved
  - No commit groupings by directory (meaningless to non-technical readers)
"""

from pathlib import Path
from backend.llm_client import generate

_PROMPT_PATH = Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / "prompts" / "client_summary.txt"
_MAX_TOKENS = 600  # narrative prose needs more room than per-commit sentences


def render_all(summary: dict) -> dict:
    """
    Run one LLM call to produce a client-facing narrative, then wrap it into
    slack / email / standup format strings.

    Returns:
        {"slack": str, "email": str, "standup": str}
    """
    narrative = _generate_narrative(summary)
    repo = summary["repo"]
    since = summary["range"]["since"]
    until = summary["range"]["until"]

    return {
        "slack":   _slack(narrative, repo, since, until),
        "email":   _email(narrative, repo, since, until),
        "standup": _standup(narrative, summary, since, until),
    }


def _generate_narrative(summary: dict) -> str:
    """Call the LLM once with all commit summaries and return the narrative."""
    prompt_template = _PROMPT_PATH.read_text()

    # Collect the developer-written per-commit summaries (already generated)
    commits_text = ""
    for group in summary["groups"]:
        for commit in group["commits"]:
            text = commit.get("summary") or commit["message"]
            commits_text += f"- {text}\n"

    if not commits_text.strip():
        return "No significant changes were found in this period."

    prompt = prompt_template.replace("{{COMMITS}}", commits_text)
    return generate(prompt, max_tokens=_MAX_TOKENS)


# ── Format wrappers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def _slack(narrative: str, repo: str, since: str, until: str) -> str:
    lines = [
        f"*📢 Product Update — `{repo}`*",
        f"_{since}  →  {until}_",
        "",
        narrative,
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


def _email(narrative: str, repo: str, since: str, until: str) -> str:
    lines = [
        f"Subject: Product Update — {repo}",
        f"Period: {since} to {until}",
        "",
        "Hi,",
        "",
        narrative,
        "",
        "Best,",
        "Standup Sync",
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)


def _standup(narrative: str, summary: dict, since: str, until: str) -> str:
    """
    Client-facing standup: one narrative paragraph per author, re-using the
    same narrative since grouping by file/directory is meaningless to clients.
    We list the authors who contributed so stakeholders know who to credit.
    """
    authors = sorted({
        commit["author"]
        for group in summary["groups"]
        for commit in group["commits"]
    })
    author_line = ", ".join(authors) if authors else "the team"

    lines = [
        f"PRODUCT UPDATE — {summary['repo']}",
        f"{since} → {until}",
        "",
        f"Contributors this period: {author_line}",
        "",
        narrative,
    ]
    return "\n".join(lines)

+    lines = [
+        f"Subject: Product Update — {repo}",
+        f"Period: {since} to {until}",
+        "",
+        "Hi,",
+        "",
+        narrative,
+        "",
+        "Best,",
+        "Standup Sync",
+    ]
+    return "\n".join(lines)
+
+
+def _standup(narrative: str, summary: dict, since: str, until: str) -> str:
+    """
+    Client-facing standup: one narrative paragraph per author, re-using the
+    same narrative since grouping by file/directory is meaningless to clients.
+    We list the authors who contributed so stakeholders know who to credit.
+    """
+    authors = sorted({
+        commit["author"]
+        for group in summary["groups"]
+        for commit in group["commits"]
+    })
+    author_line = ", ".join(authors) if authors else "the team"
+
+    lines = [
+        f"PRODUCT UPDATE — {summary['repo']}",
+        f"{since} → {until}",
+        "",
+        f"Contributors this period: {author_line}",
+        "",
+        narrative,
+    ]
+    return "\n".join(lines)

from backend.renderers import slack_renderer, email_renderer, standup_renderer

app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="frontend"), name="static")


class GenerateRequest(BaseModel):
    repo: str
    since: str = "24 hours ago"
    until: Optional[str] = None


def _event(event: str, data: dict) -> str:
    """Format a Server-Sent Event frame."""
    return f"event: {event}\ndata: {json.dumps(data)}\n\n"

@app.post("/api/generate")
def generate(req: GenerateRequest):
    """
    Full pipeline streamed as Server-Sent Events so the UI updates in real time.
    Events: progress | raw_log | result | error
    """
    def stream():
        try:
            # 1. Extract

            raw_commits = extract_commits(req.repo, req.since, req.until)
            if not raw_commits:

                    "detail": f"No commits found in '{req.repo}' since '{req.since}'. "
                              "Try a wider date range or check the repo path/URL."
                })
                return

            # Send raw log immediately so the "before" panel appears early
            raw_log = [f"{c['hash'][:7]} {c['author']} — {c['message']}" for c in raw_commits]
            yield _event("raw_log", {"lines": raw_log})

            filtered = filter_commits(raw_commits)
            if not filtered:
                yield _event("error", {
                    "detail": "All commits were filtered out (only merge commits, lock files, or "
                              "whitespace changes found). Try a wider date range."
                })
                return

            # 3. Analyze (LLM)

                "step": "llm",

            })
            analyzed = analyze_commits(filtered)

            # 4. Group

            groups = group_commits(analyzed)

            # 5. Detect blockers

            # 6. Assemble summary
            summary = build_summary(
                repo=req.repo,
                since=req.since,
                until=req.until,
                groups=groups,
                blockers=blockers,
                raw_commits=raw_commits,
            )

            yield _event("error", {"detail": traceback.format_exc()})

    return StreamingResponse(stream(), media_type="text/event-stream")

The code passes the URL string directly to `git clone`, so **anything `git clone` itself accepts will work**. Specifically:

**Accepted formats:**

| Format | Example | Works? |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub HTTPS (no `.git`) | `https://github.com/org/repo` | ✅ |
| GitHub HTTPS (with `.git`) | `https://github.com/org/repo.git` | ✅ |
| SSH / git@ URL | `git@github.com:org/repo.git` | ✅ (requires SSH key configured on the machine) |
| Any other HTTPS git host | `https://gitlab.com/org/repo` | ✅ |
| Local filesystem path | `/Users/you/projects/myrepo` | ✅ (no clone — reads directly) |

**The routing logic (line 38):**
- If the input starts with `http://`, `https://`, or `git@` → it runs `git clone` into a temp directory, then deletes it after.
- Everything else → treated as a **local path** on the machine where the server is running.

**Practical notes:**
- GitHub HTTPS URLs work with or without the trailing `.git` — git treats them the same.
- SSH URLs (`git@github.com:...`) only work if the server machine has an SSH key authorized for that repo.
- Private repos over HTTPS require credentials embedded in the URL (`https://token@github.com/org/repo`) or a credential helper configured on the server machine — there's no auth input in the UI.
- The clone uses `--depth=200`, so repos with very long histories going back further than 200 commits from HEAD may miss older commits in the date range.

data.content:
Yes — because the code passes the URL directly to `git clone`, **any host that `git clone` supports works**. The extractor doesn't care about the host at all; it only checks whether the string starts with `http://`, `https://`, or `git@` to decide "clone this" vs "treat as local path".

So these all work out of the box:

| Host | HTTPS example | SSH example |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub | `https://github.com/org/repo` | `git@github.com:org/repo.git` |
| GitLab | `https://gitlab.com/org/repo` | `git@gitlab.com:org/repo.git` |
| Bitbucket | `https://bitbucket.org/org/repo` | `git@bitbucket.org:org/repo.git` |
| Azure DevOps | `https://dev.azure.com/org/project/_git/repo` | `git@ssh.dev.azure.com:v3/org/project/repo` |
| Self-hosted GitLab/Gitea/etc. | `https://git.yourcompany.com/org/repo` | `git@git.yourcompany.com:org/repo.git` |
| Any bare git server | `https://example.com/repo.git` | `git@example.com:repo.git` |

The same caveats apply regardless of host:
- **Public repos** — just paste the URL, it works.
- **Private repos** — need either credentials in the URL (`https://token@gitlab.com/org/repo`) or a git credential helper already configured on the machine running the server.
- **SSH URLs** — require the server machine to have an SSH key authorized for that host.
- **`--depth=200`** is always used, so only the most recent 200 commits are fetched regardless of host.

No code changes needed — it already works for all of them.

data.content:
Yes — the token-in-URL approach works across all major hosts because it's standard HTTP Basic Auth that every git HTTPS server understands. However the token format is slightly different per host:

| Host | URL format with token |
|---|---|
| GitHub | `https://<token>@github.com/org/repo` |
| GitLab | `https://oauth2:<token>@gitlab.com/org/repo` |
| Bitbucket | `https://x-token-auth:<token>@bitbucket.org/org/repo` |
| Azure DevOps | `https://<anything>:<token>@dev.azure.com/org/project/_git/repo` |
| Self-hosted GitLab/Gitea | `https://oauth2:<token>@git.yourcompany.com/org/repo` |

The difference is just a prefix before the token — GitHub accepts the token directly, while GitLab/Bitbucket/Azure need a username prefix. 

**Two implementation options:**

**Option A — Single token field, user pastes the full credentialed URL themselves**
No logic needed. The UI just says "for private repos, include your token in the URL" and the tooltip explains the format per host. Simple, zero backend changes.

**Option B — Separate token field + host detection in the backend**
UI has a "Personal Access Token (optional)" field. The backend detects which host the URL points to, prepends the right prefix (`oauth2:` for GitLab, etc.), and injects the token before cloning. More polished UX, slightly more logic.

Option A is the fastest to ship and works just as well — the user only does it once and the formats are easy to document. Option B is cleaner UX but adds host-detection logic.

def _inject_token(url: str, token: str) -> str:
    """
    Inject a Personal Access Token into an HTTPS git URL using the
    correct format for each host.

    Formats:
      GitHub / Gitea / generic:  https://<token>@host/...
      GitLab (cloud + self-hosted): https://oauth2:<token>@host/...
      Bitbucket Cloud:           https://x-token-auth:<token>@host/...
      Azure DevOps:              https://pat:<token>@host/...
    """
    from urllib.parse import urlparse, urlunparse

    parsed = urlparse(url)
    host = parsed.hostname or ""

    if "gitlab" in host:
        userinfo = f"oauth2:{token}"
    elif "bitbucket" in host:
        userinfo = f"x-token-auth:{token}"
    elif "dev.azure.com" in host or "visualstudio.com" in host:
        userinfo = f"pat:{token}"
    else:
        # GitHub and everything else — token alone works as username
        userinfo = token

    # Replace netloc with credentialed version (strip any existing userinfo first)
    netloc = f"{userinfo}@{parsed.hostname}"
    if parsed.port:
        netloc += f":{parsed.port}"

    return urlunparse(parsed._replace(netloc=netloc))

main.py — FastAPI application entry point for Standup Sync.
"""

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
from fastapi.responses import FileResponse, StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Optional
import json
import traceback

from backend.git_extractor import extract_commits
from backend.noise_filter import filter_commits
from backend.diff_analyzer import analyze_commits
from backend.grouper import group_commits
from backend.blocker_detector import detect_blockers
from backend.summarizer import build_summary
from backend.renderers import slack_renderer, email_renderer, standup_renderer, client_renderer

app = FastAPI(title="Standup Sync")

# Serve the frontend
app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="frontend"), name="static")


class GenerateRequest(BaseModel):
    repo: str
    since: str = "24 hours ago"
    until: Optional[str] = None


def _event(event: str, data: dict) -> str:
    """Format a Server-Sent Event frame."""
    return f"event: {event}\ndata: {json.dumps(data)}\n\n"


@app.get("/")
def index():
    return FileResponse("frontend/index.html")


@app.post("/api/generate")
def generate(req: GenerateRequest):
    """
    Full pipeline streamed as Server-Sent Events so the UI updates in real time.
    Events: progress | raw_log | result | error
    """
    def stream():
        try:
            # 1. Extract
            yield _event("progress", {"step": "clone", "message": "Cloning / reading repo…"})
            raw_commits = extract_commits(req.repo, req.since, req.until)
            if not raw_commits:
                yield _event("error", {
                    "detail": f"No commits found in '{req.repo}' since '{req.since}'. "
                              "Try a wider date range or check the repo path/URL."
                })
                return

            # Send raw log immediately so the "before" panel appears early
            raw_log = [f"{c['hash'][:7]} {c['author']} — {c['message']}" for c in raw_commits]
            yield _event("raw_log", {"lines": raw_log})

            # 2. Filter
            yield _event("progress", {"step": "filter", "message": f"Filtering {len(raw_commits)} commits…"})
            filtered = filter_commits(raw_commits)

"""
main.py — FastAPI application entry point for Standup Sync.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
from fastapi.responses import FileResponse, StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Optional
import json
import traceback

from backend.git_extractor import extract_commits
from backend.noise_filter import filter_commits
from backend.diff_analyzer import analyze_commits
from backend.grouper import group_commits
from backend.blocker_detector import detect_blockers
from backend.summarizer import build_summary
from backend.renderers import slack_renderer, email_renderer, standup_renderer, client_renderer

app = FastAPI(title="Standup Sync")

# Serve the frontend
app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="frontend"), name="static")


class GenerateRequest(BaseModel):
    repo: str
    since: str = "24 hours ago"
    until: Optional[str] = None
    token: Optional[str] = None


def _event(event: str, data: dict) -> str:
    """Format a Server-Sent Event frame."""
    return f"event: {event}\ndata: {json.dumps(data)}\n\n"


@app.get("/")
def index():
    return FileResponse("frontend/index.html")


@app.post("/api/generate")
def generate(req: GenerateRequest):
    """
    Full pipeline streamed as Server-Sent Events so the UI updates in real time.
    Events: progress | raw_log | result | error
    """
    def stream():
        try:
            # 1. Extract
            yield _event("progress", {"step": "clone", "message": "Cloning / reading repo…"})
            raw_commits = extract_commits(req.repo, req.since, req.until, req.token)
            if not raw_commits:
                yield _event("error", {
                    "detail": f"No commits found in '{req.repo}' since '{req.since}'. "
                              "Try a wider date range or check the repo path/URL."
                })
                return

            # Send raw log immediately so the "before" panel appears early
            raw_log = [f"{c['hash'][:7]} {c['author']} — {c['message']}" for c in raw_commits]
            yield _event("raw_log", {"lines": raw_log})

            # 2. Filter
            yield _event("progress", {"step": "filter", "message": f"Filtering {len(raw_commits)} commits…"})
            filtered = filter_commits(raw_commits)
            if not filtered:
                yield _event("error", {
                    "detail": "All commits were filtered out (only merge commits, lock files, or "
                              "whitespace changes found). Try a wider date range."
                })
                return

            # 3. Analyze (LLM)
            yield _event("progress", {
                "step": "llm",
                "message": f"Analysing {len(filtered)} commits with LLM (this is the slow part)…"
            })
            analyzed = analyze_commits(filtered)

            # 4. Group
            yield _event("progress", {"step": "group", "message": "Grouping commits…"})
            groups = group_commits(analyzed)

            # 5. Detect blockers
            blockers = detect_blockers(analyzed)

            # 6. Assemble summary
            summary = build_summary(
                repo=req.repo,
                since=req.since,
                until=req.until,
                groups=groups,
                blockers=blockers,
                raw_commits=raw_commits,
            )

            # 7. Render and stream final result
            yield _event("progress", {"step": "render", "message": "Rendering output…"})
            formats_dev = {
                "slack":   slack_renderer.render(summary),
                "email":   email_renderer.render(summary),
                "standup": standup_renderer.render(summary),
            }
            formats_client = client_renderer.render_all(summary)
            yield _event("result", {
                "summary": summary,
                "formats": formats_dev,
                "formats_client": formats_client,
            })

        except Exception:
            yield _event("error", {"detail": traceback.format_exc()})

    return StreamingResponse(stream(), media_type="text/event-stream")

def health():

**[`backend/git_extractor.py`](backend/git_extractor.py)**
- `_inject_token(url, token)` — detects the host and prepends the right credential prefix before cloning:
  - GitLab → `oauth2:<token>@`

  - Azure DevOps → `pat:<token>@`
  - GitHub / everything else → `<token>@`
- `extract_commits()` gains an optional `token` param — only applied to HTTPS URLs (SSH handles auth via key, local paths need nothing)

data.content:
All checks pass. Here's what was built:

---

### What changed

**CSS** — styled the radio pills as clickable pill buttons (no visible radio circle — the pill itself fills dark when selected), disabled state for the date pickers, and the small reset button with a red hover.

**HTML** — replaced the old `<select>` + single date input with:
- A `Date Range` label + **✕ Reset** button in the header
- 5 pill-style radio options: Last 24h / 48h / 7d / 14d / 30d
- A **From / To** date picker row, disabled and greyed out while any pill is selected

**JS** — three interaction rules:
1. **Selecting a pill** → clears and disables the date pickers
2. **Clicking an already-selected pill** → deselects it, enables the date pickers (via `mousedown` + `wasChecked` trick, since native radio inputs don't fire `change` when re-clicked)
3. **Typing in either date picker** → deselects all pills
4. **✕ Reset** → clears pills + date pickers, disables pickers

**Generate logic** — if a pill is checked, `since` = its value and `until` = null. If no pill is checked, `since` = the From date (falls back to `"30 days ago"` if blank) and `until` = the To date.

data.content:
By design — the date pickers start disabled because the intended behavior is:

- **A quick-range pill is selected** → date pickers are disabled (not needed)
- **No pill is selected** → date pickers become enabled

But right now **no pill is pre-selected by default**, so the pickers are disabled with nothing active. That's a bad default state — the user lands on the form with everything grayed out and no obvious way to proceed.

The fix: **enable the date pickers by default** on page load (since no pill is selected). The pickers should only be disabled when a pill is actively checked.
Two fixes needed: **1)** enable pickers on page load, **2)** reset should also enable them (since after reset nothing is selected):

data.content: That's already implemented — the `mousedown` + `wasChecked` trick handles exactly that. Let me verify the current code is still intact:

The code is there and correct. The issue is likely that the hidden `<input type="radio">` elements aren't receiving the `mousedown` event because the visible click target is the `<span>` pill, not the input itself — so `mousedown` on the label/span never fires on the radio.

The fix is to move the `mousedown` listener to the parent `<label>` element instead:

  document.querySelectorAll('input[name="quick-range"]').forEach(radio => {
    // Track which was checked before the click so we can uncheck it
    radio.addEventListener('mousedown', () => {
      radio.dataset.wasChecked = radio.checked;
    });
    radio.addEventListener('change', () => {
      // A newly selected radio disables the custom date pickers and clears them

      document.getElementById('date-until').value = '';

        radio.checked = false;
        _setCustomRangeEnabled(true); // enable custom range when nothing is selected

data.content: The root cause: the `<input type="radio">` is hidden with `display: none` — clicks land on the `<label>` wrapping it, not on the input itself, so `mousedown` on the radio never fired. Moving both `mousedown` and `click` listeners to `radio.closest('label')` fixes it — the label is what the user actually clicks, and it still toggles the hidden radio through normal browser label-input association.

data.content:
Here's how the validation behaves:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| Both dates blank | No validation (git falls back to `30 days ago`) |
| Only From set | Valid — no Until means "up to now" |
| Only To set | Valid — no Since means git default |
| From > To | Red border on the To field + error message, **Generate blocked** |
| From = To | Valid — treated as a single day (`--since=X --until=X`) |
| From < To | Valid, clears any previous error |

The error message clears as soon as the user corrects the To date, and it's also cleared when selecting a quick-range pill (since the date pickers get wiped at that point).
